hook_text: In 1952, thousands of South Africans broke the law on purpose, then waited calmly for the police.
clip_script: 26 June 1952. A railway station in Port Elizabeth. A group of volunteers walks through the door marked Europeans only. They don't run. They don't fight. They wait to be arrested, singing. This is the Defiance Campaign. Its method was born decades earlier, when a young lawyer named Gandhi was thrown off a train in Pietermaritzburg. Break unjust laws openly. Never use violence. Accept the punishment. Over the next months, more than eight thousand people filled the jails. The government did not repeal a single law. Instead, it made protest a crime punished by prison and whipping. But the ANC grew from a few thousand members to about a hundred thousand. And a chief who refused to quit the ANC, Albert Luthuli, became its leader.
visual_style: Archive photos of volunteers giving the thumbs-up as they are arrested; a 'Europeans only' sign over a station entrance; Pietermaritzburg station at night; a crowd singing; a prison van; a portrait of Albert Luthuli; the Nobel Peace Prize medal.
pacing: Calm and deliberate, like the volunteers themselves.
